title: General Ledger
subtitle: Where every money movement in the club ends up
summary: The General Ledger keeps the books of Rollingstone Turf Club Ltd: the chart of accounts, monthly fiscal periods, manual journals and the accounting-event API that turns business events from all other modules into balanced journals using posting rules. It is also the place where architects can finally see how visible business activity becomes legal financial truth.

sections.title: Why Finance is the bullseye
sections.intro: Many experienced IT architects learn channels, APIs, cloud, security and customer journeys but never get a simple visual showing where all those business actions end up financially. Start here.
paragraphs:
What the customer sees

A member joins, a race entry fee is collected, a hospitality booking is taken, a supplier invoice arrives, or a winning ticket is paid.

What the business feels

Revenue is earned, an expense is incurred, cash moves, stock changes, or the organisation owes or is owed money.

What finance records

The impact lands in AR, AP, Treasury, and ultimately the General Ledger, which becomes the legal system of record.

sections.title: The layman explanation
items: Think of the front office as the stadium and finance as the scoreboard. Customers see the race, the betting window, the restaurant, the membership desk and the supplier deliveries; finance shows whether those activities made or lost money.
GL is the book of truth. It does not create the business event; it records the money meaning of that event so the company can measure profit, produce legal books and answer auditors.
AR means money others owe us. If the club sells on credit or raises customer invoices, the amount appears in Accounts Receivable until the cash is collected.
AP means money we owe others. If a supplier provides goods or services, the obligation appears in Accounts Payable until the club pays it.
Treasury is where cash and bank movement are managed. It cares about receipts, payments, balances and reconciliation.

For-profit organisations exist to earn profit legally. That is why understanding finance is like understanding the bullseye: it tells you how all visible business activity ultimately affects money, control and lawful reporting.

sections.title: Why solution and enterprise architects should care
items: If you design only the customer journey and ignore the financial consequence, you are seeing only half the enterprise system.
When you understand GL, AP, AR and Treasury, you can ask smarter questions about source references, idempotency, period control, reversals and auditability.

Enterprise backend finance is where many integration mistakes become visible: duplicate events, missing source references, wrong party mappings, incorrect revenue recognition, and unbalanced postings.

Learning finance gives architects a cross-industry advantage because every serious enterprise—retail, healthcare, manufacturing, logistics, insurance, hospitality or racing—must convert operations into books, profit measurement and statutory reporting.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: No module posts journals directly. When something with financial meaning happens (a horse is registered, a ticket is sold, goods are received), the module writes an accounting event into the outbox in the same database transaction. A relay sends it to the GL's POST /api/v1/accounting-events with a client-credentials token carrying SVC_GL_POST.

The GL looks up the posting rule for the event's module and code (for example RACING / RACE_ENTRY_FEE → debit 1210, credit 4500), or uses the accounts the event names, and writes a posted journal. The same source reference never posts twice.
Periods give control: a CLOSED period refuses postings, only TC_ADMIN can reopen it, and a posted journal is immutable. Corrections are made by reversal, which keeps the audit trail honest.

terms.definition: Header accounts (1000 Assets, 2000 Liabilities ...) and posting accounts beneath them. Only active posting accounts take journal lines.
One per month (2026-01 ...). OPEN, SOFT_CLOSED or CLOSED.
A balanced set of debit and credit lines. DRAFT while edited, POSTED when final, REVERSED when cancelled by a reversing journal.
A business fact from a module: module, event code, source reference, date, amount, party. The GL turns it into a journal.
Maps a module's event code to a debit and a credit account. 58 rules ship with the system.
An account a sub-ledger must agree with: 2100 for AP, 1200 / 1210 for AR, 1100 for the bank.

sections.title: Design decisions
items: Transactional outbox: the business change and its accounting event commit together, so the books can never miss a movement even when the GL is down.
Idempotent posting: the outbox is unique on (entity, module, source reference) and the GL answers 200 instead of 201 for a duplicate.
Rules as data: finance can change which accounts an event hits without a code change.

episode.title: Event-driven accounting: how thirteen modules keep one set of books
episode.hook: A ticket is sold at the window. Where does that 10 dollars land in the books, and what if the ledger is down at that moment?
objectives: Explain the transactional outbox and the relay
Read a posting rule and the journal it produces
Show period control and why posted journals are immutable
talkingPoints: Chart of accounts: header versus posting accounts
Manual journal: draft, balance check, post, reverse

Trial balance and account ledger reports
